\begin{abstract}
Developers routinely attribute the per-request cost of JSON Web Token (JWT)
validation to cryptography. We test that assumption in \LibraryName{}, a widely
used Node.js library. The signature primitive is \HostHmacString~$\mu$s of a
\HostJwtString~$\mu$s validation; \HostProbeThrows~$\mu$s
(\HostProbeShareOfCall\%) is a discarded parse, in which a string
secret is first offered to the asymmetric key parser and is resolved only after
that parse fails. Its price is set by a transitive dependency, the OpenSSL
release beneath the runtime: issued from C, the same calls cost
\CFullVThreeZeroSixteen~$\mu$s on OpenSSL \CVersionLiteralVThreeZeroSixteen{}
and \CFullVThreeFiveEight~$\mu$s on \CVersionLiteralVThreeFiveEight. The slow
case is not confined to end-of-life runtimes: Ubuntu 24.04's packaged Node.js,
linked to the system OpenSSL 3.0, pays \DistroUbuntuPenalty~$\mu$s per
validation. In a containerised service on OpenSSL 3.0, validation accounted for
\AbCpuShareOfRequestPct\% of the application's processor time per request. Of
seven JWT libraries in four languages, only this one uses a failing parse, and
only its penalty changes by an order of magnitude with the OpenSSL release. The obvious optimisation is
unsafe: the parse arrived with a key-confusion security fix, and removing it
naively fails the library's own tests. A fix that dispatches on the key material
alone passes the full suite on four runtimes, behaves identically to the stock
library in every case we tested, and removes the parse for every token,
including forged ones; so does passing a pre-parsed key, yet none of the
\SampleCallSites{} call sites in our sample does. We derive guidance for developers, library authors
and performance engineers, and release a replication package.
\end{abstract}

\begin{keyword}
Empirical study \sep performance analysis \sep software libraries
\sep root-cause analysis \sep JSON Web Token \sep OpenSSL

\section{Introduction}\label{sec:intro}

Performance engineering depends on attributing cost correctly. When a cost is
believed to belong to one component and belongs to another, optimisation
effort goes to the wrong place, and architectural remedies are adopted for
problems that could have been fixed in a few lines. Empirical studies of
performance bugs find that many stem from inefficient library usage and
avoidable redundant work, and that the fixes are small once the cause is
located~\citep{jin2012understanding,selakovic2016performance}. This paper
reports such a case on a path that runs on every request of many web
services: the validation of JSON Web Tokens (JWTs)~\citep{rfc7519}.

The usual reasoning is intuitive: validating a token means verifying a
signature, signatures are cryptography, and cryptography is expensive, so the
cost should be \emph{moved} to a sidecar proxy, a gateway or dedicated
hardware. The assumption has been tested before one layer down, where
\citet{coarfa2006performance} found RSA a minority of TLS server cost. We test
it at the application layer, in \LibraryName{}, a widely used Node.js library,
and find it wrong. A second natural explanation, that key material is
converted from a string into a key object on every call, fails as well: the
conversion costs \HostCreateSecretKey~$\mu$s.

The actual mechanism is a control-flow accident (Figure~\ref{fig:codepath}).
Given a secret that is not already a key object, the library attempts
\texttt{createPublicKey()} first and falls back to \texttt{createSecretKey()}
in the exception handler. For an HMAC secret the first call cannot succeed, so
every validation constructs and discards an OpenSSL parse failure, at
\HostProbeThrows~$\mu$s of a \HostJwtString~$\mu$s call. We call this failed
\texttt{createPublicKey()} call, including the exception that reports its
failure, the \emph{discarded parse}. Its price depends on
which OpenSSL release performs it, by more than an order of magnitude:
runtimes carrying OpenSSL~3.2 or later pay tens of microseconds, runtimes
carrying the 3.0 series pay hundreds. The 3.0 series is still the system
OpenSSL of long-term-support distributions, and Node.js as packaged by Ubuntu
24.04 links it and pays the slow price (Section~\ref{sec:distro}); so does any
image pinned to an older base layer, which is common in
practice~\citep{zerouali2019outdated}.

For software engineering the case matters for three reasons beyond the
library itself. First, the cost sits in control flow that no profiler label
names: a parse whose failure is caught and discarded appears in profiles as
OpenSSL work, and the natural reading of that attribution is
``cryptography''.
Second, its magnitude is set by a transitive dependency that application
developers do not choose directly and rarely record. Third, the obvious fix is
unsafe. The resolution block entered the library in version~9.0.0, the
release that fixed an RSA-to-HMAC key-confusion
vulnerability~\citep{auth0bulletin2022}, and the key-type checks implementing
that fix read the type of the key object it produces; removing it the obvious
way fails the library's own key-confusion tests. The code that costs the time
is the code that makes a security check work, and the coupling is not visible
from the lines being changed. The design that produces the cost (resolving key
material on every call, by way of a parse whose failure serves as a type test)
can also be named independently of \LibraryName{}, and it predicts which of
seven libraries perform a failing parse (Section~\ref{sec:rq4}).

\paragraph{Research questions}
\begin{list}{}{\setlength{\labelwidth}{2.2em}\setlength{\labelsep}{0.5em}%
  \setlength{\leftmargin}{2.7em}\setlength{\itemsep}{1pt}\setlength{\topsep}{2pt}%
  \setlength{\parsep}{0pt}\renewcommand{\makelabel}[1]{\textbf{#1}\hfill}}
\item[RQ1] Where does the per-request cost of token validation actually go?
\item[RQ2] What governs the magnitude of that cost?
\item[RQ3] Does it matter in a running containerised service, and how common is the
  pattern that avoids it?
\item[RQ4] Is the defect a property of one library, or of a design choice
  other libraries could share?
\item[RQ5] Can the cost be removed without weakening the library's
  key-confusion defence, and who can cause it to be paid?
\end{list}

\paragraph{Contributions} All are supported by measurements in the
replication package~\citep{artifact2026}.
\begin{enumerate}\setlength{\itemsep}{1pt}
\item Two independent decompositions of the validation call that locate its
      dominant component in a discarded parse, and a split of it into the
      OpenSSL parse, the V8 exception and the binding (Section~\ref{sec:rq1}).
\item A causal attribution of its magnitude to the bundled OpenSSL release,
      with the parse reissued from C against \CProbeVersionCount{} releases
      (Section~\ref{sec:rq2}).
\item Corroboration in a containerised service by cgroup CPU accounting, and a
      survey showing the avoiding pattern is rare in public code
      (Section~\ref{sec:rq3}).
\item A comparison of seven JWT libraries in four languages showing that the
      cost follows a design choice, not JWT validation as such, and a
      detector-based survey of \LibJwtInFrame{} plus \LibCryptoInFrame{}
      popular npm packages locating the failing-parse form of that choice
      (Section~\ref{sec:rq4}).
\item An analysis of why the cost cannot be removed naively, and two fixes
      that pass the library's full test suite; the simpler one, dispatching on
      the key material alone, removes the parse for every token, including
      forged ones (Section~\ref{sec:security}).
\item Guidance for developers, library authors and performance engineers,
      including the one-line change that removes the cost
      (Section~\ref{sec:implications}).
\end{enumerate}

\section{Background and related work}\label{sec:related}

\paragraph{What a validation call does} A JSON Web Token carries a header, a
payload and a signature over the first two~\citep{rfc7519}. Validating one means
decoding two segments, resolving key material into a form the cryptographic
library accepts, and verifying the signature. The middle step, key
resolution, is the subject of this paper, and it is the step most often left
implicit when validation cost is discussed.

\paragraph{Where the cost is usually attributed} Measurement of layered
enforcement in microservices concentrates on transport and proxy layers;
\citet{zhu2023dissecting} show that service-mesh sidecar overhead depends on
configuration and workload rather than being a fixed tax. Work on
cryptographic library performance has largely stayed at the level of the
primitive or the protocol
exchange~\citep{naser2020performance,sikeridis2020assessing}. Our result
concerns neither: it is the cost of getting key material \emph{into} the
library, which we could not find measured directly.

\paragraph{Performance bugs and anti-patterns} \citet{jin2012understanding}
found that most real-world performance bugs follow a few recurring patterns,
among them skippable function calls, and that fixes are usually local;
\citet{nistor2013discovering} found that most are discovered by reasoning about
code rather than by observing symptoms. In JavaScript,
\citet{selakovic2016performance} identify inefficient API usage as a leading
root cause, and their later profiler~\citep{selakovic2017actionable} targets the
\emph{order} in which a program evaluates conditions, the axis on which this
defect lives. The defect here is a skippable call whose failure is its only
observable effect.

\paragraph{Exceptions as control flow} Exceptions are costly in managed
runtimes, mostly in their construction~\citep{ogasawara2006edo}, and
\citet{parravicini2021cost} provide the closest cost-attribution baseline for
V8, though on speculation rather than exceptions. Studies of how exceptions are used find handlers that discard what they
catch to be common~\citep{cabral2007exception,kery2016examining,depadua2017prevalence}.
That literature treats a swallowed exception as a maintainability smell; here
it is control flow on a hot path, and Section~\ref{sec:granularity} measures
how much of its cost is the exception itself.

\paragraph{Dependencies and the npm ecosystem} Performance changes across
versions in ways maintainers do not
anticipate~\citep{kaltenecker2023performance,chen2017exploratory}. Container
images pin a dependency set implicitly~\citep{cito2017empirical} and routinely
ship outdated packages~\citep{zerouali2019outdated}. In the npm ecosystem,
\citet{staicu2018freezing} show that a slow path inside widely used modules
reaches the web servers that depend on them, and \citet{davis2018sense} that on
Node.js's single event loop one slow synchronous handler delays every other
client. For OpenSSL~3, maintainers of a
major downstream library have stated that parsing and key loading regressed
against 1.1.1~\citep{pyca2026stateofopenssl}; Section~\ref{sec:rq2-causal}
supplies a controlled measurement for the one path this paper concerns.

\paragraph{Benchmarking pitfalls and change detection} Our protocol follows
established guidance for managed-runtime
benchmarking~\citep{georges2007statistically,kalibera2013rigorous,barrett2017warmup}.
Microbenchmarks go wrong in recurring ways~\citep{costa2021wrong}, developers
misjudge when warm-up ends~\citep{traini2023steady}, cloud environments degrade
their reliability~\citep{laaber2019cloud}, and benchmark suites often fail to
detect performance changes at all~\citep{laaber2018evaluation}. The attribution
this paper overturns has the structure \citet{mytkowicz2009wrong} warn about: a
second variable, the bundled OpenSSL version, moving unrecorded alongside the
one under study.

\paragraph{Security and performance} Security mechanisms are routinely
evaluated for their performance cost: \citet{coarfa2006performance} for TLS
servers, and \citet{sikeridis2020assessing} for post-quantum TLS and SSH. In
that line the cost is the price of the protection. Here the cost and the
protection are coupled in a less visible way: the code that costs the time is
the code a security check depends on (Section~\ref{sec:fix}).

\paragraph{Cryptographic APIs and JWT libraries} Most cryptographic
vulnerabilities are misuses of libraries by applications~\citep{lazar2014why,egele2013empirical},
largely because the interfaces are hard to use~\citep{nadi2016jumping};
detection has been automated by specifying correct
usage~\citep{kruger2018crysl,rahaman2019cryptoguard}. Our finding differs: the
interface admits a use that is \emph{correct} and costly only for a reason
invisible at the call site. Security analyses of JWT implementations
consistently find key-handling defects, key confusion among
them~\citep{detering2017jose,xu2023jwtkey}; \citet{yang2026tokentimebomb}
evaluated 43 JWT libraries across 16 languages. RFC
8725~\citep{rfc8725} codifies the resulting practice. The library studied here
has been hardened against key confusion twice: CVE-2015-9235, fixed in
4.2.2~\citep{ghsa2015jsonwebtoken}, and CVE-2022-23541 with two related
defects, fixed in 9.0.0~\citep{auth0bulletin2022}. We treat the same surface
as a cost site and show the two views are coupled. Our survey follows
guidance on mining public repositories~\citep{kalliamvakou2014promises}.

We found no peer-reviewed study of performance regressions across the
OpenSSL~3.x series, none tracing the chain from base image to bundled library
to application performance, and none treating a correct-but-costly use of a
cryptographic interface as a performance defect. We state each as an absence
we searched for.

\subsection{Testbed}\label{sec:testbed}

Unless stated otherwise, measurements were taken on one Apple-silicon machine
running macOS~26.5.2 (arm64), \emph{the host}, under Node.js~v26.6.0. This
Node.js is the Homebrew build, which links the system's Homebrew OpenSSL
dynamically rather than bundling its own; the host therefore ran OpenSSL
\HostOpensslInferred, newer than the 3.5 series that official Node~26 builds
bundle. The version was not recorded per row for the host decomposition, and
is inferred from the run record (Section~\ref{sec:threats}). Container
measurements ran in the Linux/arm64 virtual machine of Docker Desktop's
single-node Kubernetes cluster (v1.32.2). The service studied in
Section~\ref{sec:rq3} is a Node.js microservice (Express~5.1.0,
\LibraryName{}~9.0.3) on the \texttt{node:18-alpine} image, run as one replica
with an Istio sidecar behind an NGINX ingress, verifying HS256 tokens with a
shared secret supplied as a string. Load was generated in open loop by
k6~v2.2.0 on the same machine, so every in-situ window records the host load
average observed during it. This is a controlled single-node testbed, not a
production deployment; we call it the \emph{containerised service}.

Table~\ref{tab:machines} lists every machine that produced a reported value.
Absolute timings are comparable only within one machine; across machines we
compare orderings and ratios. The x86\_64 runs used two different cloud VMs:
VM~A, for the runs of the first revision, was no longer available when the
second set of runs was made on VM~B, so those could not be repeated on VM~A.

\subsection{Measurement protocol}\label{sec:unit}

The unit of measurement is one operating-system process, not one call. Each
process performs a fixed number of timed iterations of a single condition after
a warmup of half that number and contributes its median; reported figures are
medians of per-process medians, with 95\% percentile bootstrap intervals over
processes (\BootstrapResamples{} resamples)~\citep{georges2007statistically}.
With \HostInvocations{} processes per condition these intervals are indicative
rather than calibrated; the per-process values are in the replication package,
and its analysis script can also report BCa intervals. Conditions are interleaved within
each round, and differences between conditions are reported as the median of
per-round \emph{paired} differences. The largest between-process coefficient of
variation is \HostCvMax\% on the host.

\subsection{Instruments}\label{sec:decompose}

\paragraph{Decomposing the call} \texttt{jwt.verify()} of \LibraryName{}
\LibraryVersion{} is decomposed into the operations it performs, each timed in
isolation: structural decode, the HMAC primitive with a string and with a
pre-parsed key, the symmetric key constructor, and the asymmetric key parse the
library attempts first (Figure~\ref{fig:codepath}), both when it throws and
when it succeeds. Each condition runs in \HostInvocations{} processes of
\HostCallsPerInvocation{} calls.

\begin{figure}[!t]
\lstinputlisting[firstnumber=\CodeFirstLine]{figures/codepath_excerpt.js}
\caption{Key resolution in \LibraryName{} \LibraryVersion{},
\texttt{\CodeFileLines}. Verbatim but for the common leading indentation,
which is removed to fit the column; line numbers are the file's own. A secret
that is not already a \texttt{KeyObject} is offered to
\texttt{createPublicKey()} first, and \texttt{createSecretKey()} is reached only
from the exception handler. For an HMAC secret supplied as a string the outer
\texttt{try} can never succeed, so the asymmetric parse is attempted and
discarded on every validation.}
\label{fig:codepath}
\end{figure}

\paragraph{Runtime matrix}\label{sec:matrix-method} Containerisation is held
constant and the runtime varied: four container images spanning two OpenSSL
series and three V8 major versions, on one machine, at \MatrixInvocations{}
processes of \MatrixCallsPerInvocation{} calls. The runtime identity of each
image is recorded with every row and cross-checked (\IdentityMismatches{}
mismatches).

\paragraph{C probe}\label{sec:c-method} To remove the JavaScript engine, we
reproduced in C, call for call from the Node source, what
\texttt{createPublicKey()} asks of OpenSSL for an HMAC secret (three PEM scans,
a private-key parse and the error-queue drain), compiled with one compiler
(\CProbeCompiler) against \CProbeVersionCount{} OpenSSL releases from
\CProbeVersionFirst{} to \CProbeVersionLast{} built identically from source,
at \CProbeInvocations{} processes per release.

\paragraph{Exception baseline}\label{sec:exc-method} An \texttt{Error} of the
same message, properties and code as Node's (captured from a real failure) is
thrown from \ExcDepth{} frames and discarded, with no OpenSSL call, on six
official Node runtimes. With the C probe this gives a three-way decomposition
of the discarded parse: the OpenSSL parse, the V8 exception, and a remainder
attributed to the binding between them.

\paragraph{Other libraries}\label{sec:xlib-method} We read the key-handling
code of six further libraries, the most used in their ecosystems
(\texttt{fast-jwt}, \texttt{jose}, \texttt{PyJWT}, \texttt{golang-jwt},
\texttt{nimbus-jose-jwt}, \texttt{jjwt}), and timed HS256 verification in each
with the secret as a string (or the rawest accepted form) and as the library's
own pre-parsed key object, at \XlibInvocations{} processes of
\XlibCallsPerInvocation{} calls.

\paragraph{Second architecture}\label{sec:arch-method} The host decomposition,
the runtime matrix, the C probe, the exception baseline and the cross-library
comparison were measured on an x86\_64 virtual machine (\ExcCpuModel, four
vCPUs) on shared cloud infrastructure. Following \citet{laaber2019cloud}, we take
only orderings and ratios between interleaved conditions from it. Two Node~22
builds appear in these runs: the repetition of the host decomposition used that
machine's own Node \XhNode{} (OpenSSL \XhOpenssl), while the exception baseline
used the official Node \RtTwentyTwoLiteral{} release binary, which bundles
OpenSSL \RtTwentyTwoOpenssl.

\paragraph{In-situ measurement}\label{sec:insitu-method} The containerised
service exposes a histogram timing the verification call alone, read before and
after each of seven arrival-rate steps; means are exact differences of
\texttt{\_sum} over \texttt{\_count}. The sweep ran twice on one process,
ascending then descending. An A/B at one rate, validation enabled and then
disabled, reads the processor time charged to the container from cgroup
accounting.

\paragraph{Prevalence}\label{sec:frames} Three instruments with different
frames, captured on \PopCapturedAt: code-search co-occurrence counts, a
classified convenience sample of call sites (one file per repository, key
argument traced within its file), and a targeted counter-search that fetches
every file co-occurring the library with the pre-parsing interface and
adjudicates it by hand. None supports a population proportion, so results are
reported \emph{in our sample}.

\paragraph{Distribution-packaged Node.js} To test whether the OpenSSL~3.0 case
survives on supported systems, an Ubuntu 24.04 image with the distribution's
own \texttt{nodejs} package, which links the system OpenSSL, is measured beside
two official images under the runtime-matrix protocol (Section~\ref{sec:distro}).

\paragraph{Rejected tokens} A further harness times \texttt{verify()} on
well-formed tokens that the client can build without the secret, one declaring
RS256 and one declaring HS256 with a signature not made with the secret, under
the stock library, both fixes of Section~\ref{sec:fix} and a pre-parsed key;
a second script compares the stock library and each fix on every combination
of key material, token and algorithm option; and the library's own test suite
is run against each variant on every runtime (Section~\ref{sec:reachable}).

\paragraph{Library survey}\label{sec:libsurvey-method} To move RQ4 from
existence towards prevalence, a frame of npm packages is drawn from the
registry's search interface with stated queries and a weekly-download
threshold, and a detector built on a JavaScript parser flags every
\texttt{try}/\texttt{catch} whose \texttt{try} calls a key or certificate
parser and whose handler falls back to a different key constructor. Every hit is
read and adjudicated by hand (Section~\ref{sec:libsurvey}).

Table~\ref{tab:host} and Figure~\ref{fig:decomposition} give each operation in
the validation path. The signature primitive costs \HostHmacString~$\mu$s of a
\HostJwtString~$\mu$s call. The conversion to which the remainder is most
readily attributed, the symmetric key constructor, costs
\HostCreateSecretKey~$\mu$s. The discarded parse that precedes it costs
\HostProbeThrows~$\mu$s, \HostProbeShareOfCall\% of the call and its largest
single component. Supplying a pre-parsed key instead of a string reduces the
call by \HostStringPenalty~$\mu$s [\HostStringPenaltyCiLo,
\HostStringPenaltyCiHi]. The asymmetry often read as conversion being dearer
than parsing is backwards: a \emph{successful} asymmetric parse costs
\HostProbeSucceeds~$\mu$s, so the RSA path's parse is useful work while the
HMAC path's is waste.

Table~\ref{tab:decomp} decomposes the discarded parse on six official runtimes. On every
runtime bundling OpenSSL~3.0 the C parse alone matches the probe to within a
few percent (\RtEighteenDecompCPct\% of it under Node \RtEighteenLiteral): the
discarded parse \emph{is} the OpenSSL parse and would cost the same with no
JavaScript engine. The V8 exception is small and nearly constant, about
\RtEighteenExcNodeLike~$\mu$s (\RtEighteenDecompExcPct\% of the probe under Node
\RtEighteenLiteral), half of it stack capture. Where OpenSSL~3.5 makes the parse
cheap, the three parts are comparable: under Node \RtTwentySixLiteral{} the
parse is \RtTwentySixDecompCPct\%, the exception \RtTwentySixDecompExcPct\% and
the binding \RtTwentySixDecompLeftoverPct\%. The three-way split is
interpretable only for these OpenSSL~3.5 rows. On the OpenSSL~3.0 rows the
binding comes out negative (\RtEighteenDecompLeftover~$\mu$s under Node
\RtEighteenLiteral), because our stock C build of each release and Node's own
build of it differ by more than the binding costs; there only the dominance of
the parse is meaningful. Either way the component is a discarded
\emph{parse}, not an exception cost.

\subsection{Checks on the decomposition}\label{sec:residual}

The discarded parse and the conversion account for \DecompExplainedPct\% of the
string penalty. The \DecompResidual~$\mu$s residual [\DecompResidualCiLo,
\DecompResidualCiHi] presumably lies in the library's own type and claim
checking, but it was not measured directly and is reported as unattributed.
Because the decomposition relies on differencing, it was checked against V8's
sampling profiler: the asymmetric key parse accounts for a median
\ProfHostPct\% of self time on the host (\ProfEighteenPct\% under Node
\NodeEighteenNodeMajor{} and \ProfTwentySixPct\% under Node
\NodeTwentySixMuslNodeMajor), and does not appear among the top frames of the
pre-parsed path. The two methods agree on which component dominates, not on
its exact share: differencing gives \HostProbeShareOfCall\% and the profiler
\ProfHostPct\% on the host. They measure different quantities. The differenced
share divides the median of the parse, timed alone in its own processes, by
the median of the whole call; the profiler's share attributes sampled time
inside one validation loop to the innermost frame, so work the parse frame
triggers (including the construction of its exception) is counted with it, and
sampling carries attribution error of its own~\citep{mytkowicz2010profilers}.
We therefore rely on the ordering, not on either percentage.

\subsection{What the runtime matrix shows}\label{sec:cannot-separate}

Table~\ref{tab:matrix} varies the runtime with containerisation held constant.
The discarded parse spans \SpanProbeThrows$\times$ across the four images, while
pre-parsed validation spans only \SpanJwtPreparsed$\times$. Node
\NodeEighteenNodeMajor{} and Node \NodeTwentyNodeMajor{} ship different V8
major versions and share the OpenSSL \NodeEighteenOpensslSeries{} series; both
pay of order \NodeEighteenProbeThrows--\NodeTwentyProbeThrows~$\mu$s, so within
that series the engine does not move the cost. A successful parse moves with the
failing one (\SpanProbeSucceeds$\times$), so the effect concerns key parsing in
general. The matrix alone cannot separate OpenSSL from the engine across the
series boundary, since the fast images also carry a newer engine and a
different build; the crossed designs below do.

\subsection{Caused by OpenSSL}\label{sec:rq2-causal}

\begin{figure}[!t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{fig_openssl_releases.pdf}
\caption{The failed parse of an HMAC secret issued from C, with no JavaScript
engine, against \CProbeVersionCount{} OpenSSL releases built from source with
one configuration, beside a
successful parse of an RSA-2048 public key through the same path. Whiskers are
95\% percentile bootstrap intervals over \CProbeInvocations{} processes and
are narrower than the markers. The cost falls in two steps, at 3.1 and 3.2,
and is flat thereafter.}
\label{fig:openssl}
\end{figure}

In plain C, with nothing else varying, the failure costs
\CFullVThreeZeroSixteen~$\mu$s on OpenSSL \CVersionLiteralVThreeZeroSixteen{}
and \CFullVThreeFiveEight~$\mu$s on \CVersionLiteralVThreeFiveEight, a ratio of
\CFullRatioOldNew{} [\CFullRatioOldNewCiLo, \CFullRatioOldNewCiHi]
(Figure~\ref{fig:openssl}). The magnitude is therefore \emph{caused} by the
OpenSSL release, for this code path. Almost all of it is the private-key parse
(\CPrivateShareVThreeZeroSixteen\% on \CVersionLiteralVThreeZeroSixteen), where
OpenSSL~3 hands the input to its provider-based decoders. The cost fell in two
steps, to \CFullVThreeOneEight~$\mu$s in \CVersionLiteralVThreeOneEight{} and to
\CFullVThreeTwoSix~$\mu$s in \CVersionLiteralVThreeTwoSix, and is flat
thereafter. The engine is excluded from the other direction too: Node
\RtTwentyThreeLiteral{} pairs a \emph{newer} V8 with the \emph{older} OpenSSL
\RtTwentyThreeOpenssl{} and pays \RtTwentyThreeProbe~$\mu$s, against
\RtTwentyTwoProbe~$\mu$s for Node \RtTwentyTwoLiteral{} with OpenSSL
\RtTwentyTwoOpenssl.

\paragraph{A second architecture}\label{sec:rq2-arch} On x86\_64 every
OpenSSL~3.0 image is again slower than every OpenSSL~3.5 image (the split
\XmSeriesSplitHolds): the discarded parse spans \XmSpanProbeThrows$\times$ across
the images while pre-parsed validation spans \XmSpanJwtPreparsed$\times$. The
host decomposition keeps its ordering: the discarded parse is
\XhProbeThrows~$\mu$s of a \XhJwtString~$\mu$s call (\XhProbeShareOfCall\%).

\subsection{Distribution-packaged Node.js}\label{sec:distro}

The OpenSSL~3.0 series is not confined to end-of-life Node.js images. Ubuntu
24.04 LTS packages Node.js \DistroUbuntuNode{}, built against the system's
shared OpenSSL rather than a bundled copy; in its current image that is OpenSSL
\DistroUbuntuOpenssl. The package (\texttt{\UbuntuNodejsPkg}) is in the
\emph{\UbuntuNodejsComponent} component, which Ubuntu describes as
``community and extra packages'' whose security coverage is provided by
Expanded Security Maintenance through Ubuntu Pro, and the archive held no newer
version on
\UbuntuNodejsCaptured.\footnote{\url{https://ubuntu.com/about/release-cycle};
the package record and the page excerpt are in the replication package.} It is
nonetheless what \texttt{apt install nodejs} installs on a current LTS system.
Debian 12's packaged Node.js could not be measured: the Debian archive was not
reachable from VM~B, and the run is scripted in the replication package.
Table~\ref{tab:distro} measures it beside two of the
official images of Table~\ref{tab:matrix}, on one x86\_64 virtual machine
(\DistroCpus{} vCPUs) in one run (\DistroCaptured), with the protocol of
Section~\ref{sec:unit}.

On Ubuntu 24.04's own Node.js the discarded parse costs
\DistroUbuntuProbeThrows~$\mu$s, the same order as on the end-of-life
\texttt{node:18} image measured alongside it (\DistroRefEighteenProbeThrows~$\mu$s)
and an order of magnitude above the OpenSSL~3.5 image
(\DistroRefTwentySixProbeThrows~$\mu$s). Supplying the secret as a string costs
\DistroUbuntuPenalty~$\mu$s per validation [\DistroUbuntuPenaltyCiLo,
\DistroUbuntuPenaltyCiHi] against a pre-parsed key; the narrow fix brings the
call to \DistroUbuntuJwtStringSafe~$\mu$s and the key-material fix of
Section~\ref{sec:fix} to \DistroUbuntuJwtStringKeyonly~$\mu$s. The OpenSSL~3.0 price is
therefore not an artefact of end-of-life images: a service that runs the Node.js
its LTS distribution ships pays it today. How many deployments do so we cannot
say; we have no data on the runtimes \LibraryName{} users deploy.

\section{RQ3: The containerised service, and prevalence}\label{sec:rq3}

\subsection{In-situ cost}\label{sec:insitu}

\begin{figure}[!t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.72\columnwidth]{fig_insitu_rate.pdf}
\caption{In-situ validation cost against arrival rate, string secret. The two
passes are drawn separately rather than averaged, because they differ
systematically and averaging would conceal that. The shaded
band is the range between the passes, which is two observations rather than an
interval.}
\label{fig:insitu}
\end{figure}

Figure~\ref{fig:insitu} shows the in-situ cost at seven arrival rates. The cost
is present in the containerised service and far larger than the host figure,
consistent with Section~\ref{sec:rq2}: the service's runtime carries the older
OpenSSL, whose discarded parse costs \NodeEighteenProbeThrows~$\mu$s, giving an
expected total near \InsituPredictedFromMatrix~$\mu$s. Wall-clock means of
\InsituObservedLo--\InsituObservedHi~$\mu$s exceed that; contention inflates
durations, so they are upper bounds. Two features of Figure~\ref{fig:insitu}
are not explained by validation and we draw no conclusion from them. The cost
falls as the arrival rate rises, and the descending pass differs from the
ascending one systematically rather than randomly. Plausible causes, none of
which we isolated, are a fixed per-window overhead amortised over more calls at
higher rates; processor frequency scaling and idle-state exit latency, which
penalise sparse arrivals; cache and branch-predictor residency, which improve
with call density; and continued JIT tier-up and garbage-collection timing,
which differ between a process's first and second pass. The magnitude claim
rests instead on the processor-time measurement below.

\subsection{Corroboration: the cost is processor time}\label{sec:abcorroboration}

\begin{table*}[!htbp]
\caption{Validation enabled against validation disabled, at one arrival rate,
two \AbWindowSecondsJwt~s windows on the same pod and image, \AbRequestsNone{}
requests each. A signed token is on the wire in both arms; the disabled arm
removes only the handler's \texttt{jwt.verify()} call. Application and sidecar
CPU are means of one-second cgroup samples in the window; CPU per call is that
mean divided by the achieved rate. Event-loop lag is the mean of the
per-scrape p99. Host load is a single sample at window start.}
\label{tab:ab}
\begin{tabular*}{\textwidth}{@{\extracolsep{\fill}}lrr@{}}
\toprule
 & disabled & enabled \\
\midrule
Achieved rate (req/s)              & \AbRateNone                & \AbRateJwt \\
Application CPU (millicores)       & \AbCpuNone                 & \AbCpuJwt \\
\textbf{CPU per call ($\mu$s)}     & \textbf{\AbCpuPerCallNone} & \textbf{\AbCpuPerCallJwt} \\
Sidecar CPU (millicores)           & \AbSidecarCpuNone          & \AbSidecarCpuJwt \\
Event-loop lag (ms)                & \AbEventLoopLagNone        & \AbEventLoopLagJwt \\

Host load, 1 min                   & \AbLoadOneNone             & \AbLoadOneJwt \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular*}
\end{table*}

To separate work from waiting, Table~\ref{tab:ab} compares the same service with
validation enabled and disabled, reading processor time from cgroup accounting
rather than from a clock. Enabling validation raised the application's
processor time per request from \AbCpuPerCallNone{} to \AbCpuPerCallJwt~$\mu$s:
validation accounted for \AbCpuShareOfRequestPct\% of the application's CPU per
request, a factor of \AbCpuRatio{} over the service without it. The added
\AbCpuPerCallDelta~$\mu$s is of the same size as the
\InsituPredictedFromMatrix~$\mu$s the runtime matrix predicts for the same work
on the same runtime, from instruments that share no code. A request that
queues accrues wall-clock time but no CPU, so this figure excludes queueing
delay; it can still be inflated by contention for caches, SMT siblings and
processor frequency on the shared host. The sidecar's CPU did not rise with the
application's, and the one-second CPU samples of the two arms do not overlap
(disabled never exceeded \AbCpuSampleMaxNone{} millicores, enabled never fell
below \AbCpuSampleMinJwt). This is one pair of consecutive windows at different
host load, so the difference carries no interval; a repeated, alternating
design is prepared for the authors' testbed (Section~\ref{sec:threats}).

\subsection{How common is the avoiding pattern, in our sample?}\label{sec:prevalence}

\begin{figure}[!t]
\centering
\input{figures/fig_survey_keysource.tex}
\caption{Where the secret passed to the validator comes from, for the
\SampleCallSites{} call sites classified in our sample. No call site passes a
pre-parsed key object, the one form that avoids the discarded parse for every
input. Independently, \SampleNoAlgorithms{} of the \SampleCallSites{} call
sites (\SampleNoAlgorithmsPct\%) pass no algorithm restriction. Counts
describe the sample, not the population (Section~\ref{sec:frames}).}
\label{fig:survey}
\end{figure}

In code-search counts, no cell exceeds \PopWorstCellPct\% of files importing
the library that also mention the pre-parsing interface. Of \SampleCallSites{}
call sites classified across \SampleRepos{} repositories, \SampleSitesPreparsed{}
pass a pre-parsed key (Figure~\ref{fig:survey}), and \SampleNoAlgorithms{}
(\SampleNoAlgorithmsPct\%) pass no algorithm restriction. Call sites are found by
resolving the local binding of the import, which adds \SampleRematchAdded{} that
the conventional \texttt{jwt.verify()} spelling misses. The targeted
counter-search fetched \CounterFilesFetched{} files, \CounterWithVerify{} with a
validation call in \CounterReposWithVerify{} repositories. Of the
\AdjudicatedTotal{} call sites it flagged automatically, hand inspection found
\AdjudicatedFalsePositive{} false positives and \AdjudicatedUnresolved{} that
could not be resolved within its file; \AdjudicatedGenuine{} were genuine, in
\AdjudicatedGenuineProjects{} projects. Even among repositories that know the
interface exists, only \AdjudicatedGenuinePct\% use it: the pattern is rare, not
absent. The zero in the classified sample may be biased downwards: keys are
traced within one file only, and \SampleUnknown{} of the \SampleCallSites{}
call sites pass an identifier whose origin lies in another file and could, in
principle, be a key object built there. No file in the sample mentions the
pre-parsing interface in any spelling, which weighs against that, but it is not
proof.

\section{RQ4: One library, or a design choice?}\label{sec:rq4}

A cost found in one library becomes a statement about a class of defect only if
its mechanism can be named independently and predicts which other libraries
have it. The mechanism here is \emph{resolving key material of unknown type by
attempting the asymmetric parse first, and treating its failure as the signal
that the material is a shared secret}. Table~\ref{tab:xlib} and
Figure~\ref{fig:xlib} test that prediction.

\begin{table*}[!t]

documentation shows, and in the library's own key object built once

$^{a}$No string accepted for an HMAC key; the rawest accepted form (bytes) is

\begin{figure}[!t]
\centering
\input{figures/fig_xlib_ratio.tex}
\caption{How much each library pays for being handed its raw secret rather
than its own pre-parsed key object: the ratio of the two costs in
Table~\ref{tab:xlib}, on a log scale. A ratio of one (dashed line) means no
per-call penalty. Orange: the paired 95\% interval on the penalty excludes
zero. \LibraryName{} and \texttt{jose} both pay for per-call key handling;
under OpenSSL~3.5.8 their absolute penalties are indistinguishable, and
\LibraryName{}'s larger ratio there reflects \texttt{jose}'s higher baseline.
Only \LibraryName{} performs a failing asymmetric parse, and only its penalty
changes by an order of magnitude with the OpenSSL release.}
\label{fig:xlib}
\end{figure}

Only \LibraryName{} attempts the asymmetric parse. The others avoid it in one of
three ways: \emph{inspect, then dispatch} (\texttt{fast-jwt} and \texttt{PyJWT}
examine the key text and call exactly one constructor); \emph{refuse the
ambiguous input} (\texttt{jose} and \texttt{golang-jwt} do not accept a string
HMAC key); or \emph{type the key} (\texttt{jjwt} requires a \texttt{SecretKey};
\texttt{nimbus-jose-jwt} converts a string's bytes without parsing them).

Of the \XlibLibCount{} libraries, \XlibPenaltyLibCount{} pay for a raw secret,
in the sense that the paired interval on the penalty excludes zero; the other
\XlibZeroPenaltyLibCount{} pay nothing measurable. The two are \LibraryName{}
and \texttt{jose}, and they pay for different reasons. \texttt{jose} parses
nothing that can fail, but imports raw bytes into a WebCrypto key on every
call. Under \XlibJsonwebtokenNewSslBackend{} the two absolute penalties are
statistically indistinguishable: \XlibJsonwebtokenNewSslPenalty~$\mu$s
[\XlibJsonwebtokenNewSslPenaltyCiLo, \XlibJsonwebtokenNewSslPenaltyCiHi] for
\LibraryName{} and \XlibJoseNewSslPenalty~$\mu$s [\XlibJoseNewSslPenaltyCiLo,
\XlibJoseNewSslPenaltyCiHi] for \texttt{jose}. \LibraryName{}'s larger ratio in
Figure~\ref{fig:xlib} there reflects \texttt{jose}'s higher baseline, not a
larger penalty. The libraries separate under \XlibJsonwebtokenOldSslBackend:
\LibraryName{}'s penalty rises to \XlibJsonwebtokenOldSslPenalty~$\mu$s and
\texttt{jose}'s to \XlibJoseOldSslPenalty~$\mu$s, about \XlibJwtOverJoseOldSsl{}
times less. The distinguishing property of \LibraryName{} is therefore not that
it alone pays for per-call key handling, but that it does so through a
\emph{failing} parse, whose price follows the OpenSSL release by an order of
magnitude. All seven libraries validate the same kind of token with the same
primitive, so the cost follows a design choice, resolving key material on every
call, and not JWT validation as such. The failing parse is the form of that
choice most exposed to the cryptographic library underneath, and the class of
order-of-evaluation defect the profiler of \citet{selakovic2017actionable}
targets.

\subsection{How often is a failing parse used as a type test?}\label{sec:libsurvey}

Seven libraries show that the design choice exists; they do not show how often
it is made. We therefore searched for it systematically in one ecosystem
(Section~\ref{sec:libsurvey-method}). The first frame holds the npm packages
returned for six JWT and JOSE keyword queries with at least \LibJwtThreshold{}
weekly downloads (\LibJwtInFrame{} of \LibJwtReturned{} returned, captured
\LibJwtCaptured); the second, wider frame holds packages returned for nine
cryptography, signature, certificate and authentication queries with at least
\LibCryptoThreshold{} weekly downloads (\LibCryptoInFrame{} of
\LibCryptoReturned). The detector parsed all \LibJwtFiles{} and
\LibCryptoFiles{} JavaScript files of the published tarballs without parse
failures in either frame.

It flagged \LibJwtPkgsAnyHit{} package in the first frame and
\LibCryptoPkgsAnyHit{} in the second. The one package is \LibraryName{}
itself, at \LibJwtConfirmed{} sites, both confirmed by reading and both on a
per-call path: the \texttt{verify()} block studied here, and the same shape in
\texttt{sign()}, which offers the configured secret to
\texttt{createPrivateKey()} before falling back to \texttt{createSecretKey()}.
Signing therefore pays a discarded parse too. Timed on the runtimes of
Table~\ref{tab:distro}, \texttt{sign()} with a string secret costs
\DistroUbuntuSignString~$\mu$s on Ubuntu 24.04's Node.js, against
\DistroUbuntuSignPreparsed~$\mu$s with a pre-parsed key (a paired penalty of
\DistroUbuntuSignPenalty~$\mu$s [\DistroUbuntuSignPenaltyCiLo,
\DistroUbuntuSignPenaltyCiHi]); \DistroRefEighteenSignString{} against
\DistroRefEighteenSignPreparsed~$\mu$s on \texttt{node:18.20.8-alpine}; and
\DistroRefTwentySixSignString{} against \DistroRefTwentySixSignPreparsed~$\mu$s
on \texttt{node:26.6.0-alpine}. An issuer that signs with a string secret on
OpenSSL~3.0 pays the same order of cost as a verifier. Within these
frames, then, the failing parse used as a type test is not a common idiom but a
property of one library, whose reach comes from that library's own adoption.
The detector matches one syntactic shape, so a type test written differently
(for example by inspecting an error code, or through a third-party parser) is
not flagged, and the count is a lower bound within the frames; other
ecosystems remain to be surveyed.

%% ============================================================================
\section{RQ5: Removing the cost safely}\label{sec:security}

\subsection{Threat model, and the discarded parse precedes authentication}\label{sec:threatmodel}\label{sec:preauth}

The adversary is a remote client that can place arbitrary bytes where the
service expects a bearer token, including every header field, but does not know
the shared secret. The asset is key-type separation: a token declaring an HMAC
algorithm must never be verified against asymmetric key material, nor the
reverse~\citep{rfc8725}. We measure what a rejected forged token costs per
call (Section~\ref{sec:reachable}), but we drove no adversarial traffic at a
service and make no claim about availability or capacity. Figure~\ref{fig:verifyorder} shows the order of checks in
\texttt{verify()}. Reaching key resolution requires only a well-formed token;
the permitted-algorithm list, the key-type checks and the signature all come
later. A token that will be rejected therefore pays the discarded parse in
full, and restricting permitted algorithms does not avoid it.

\begin{figure}[!t]
\centering
\input{figures/fig_verify_order.tex}
\caption{Order of operations in \texttt{verify()} at \LibraryTag, with the
file's line numbers. Every step up to and including the algorithm and key-type
checks runs before the signature is verified, and so runs for a forged token
exactly as for a genuine one. The discarded parse sits inside key
resolution; the key-type checks that implement the library's key-confusion
defence read the type of the key object resolution produces (dashed arrow).
Pinning permitted algorithms is enforced at the third step and therefore does
not prevent the second.}
\label{fig:verifyorder}
\end{figure}

\subsection{The discarded parse arrived with a key-confusion fix}\label{sec:provenance}

Comparing \texttt{verify.js} in versions 8.5.1, 9.0.0 and 9.0.3: in 8.5.1 the
secret is passed to the signature routine as given, and the resolution block of
Figure~\ref{fig:codepath} first appears in 9.0.0, the release that fixed
CVE-2022-23541 and CVE-2022-23539~\citep{auth0bulletin2022}. The checks
implementing those fixes (lines 148--160) operate on the key object the block
produces. The discarded parse is part of a security fix, not an oversight.

\subsection{Two fixes, and a constraint on both}\label{sec:fix}

\begin{figure}[!t]
\centering
\input{figures/fig_remedies.tex}
\caption{Per-call HS256 validation cost with a string secret under the stock
library, the narrow fix and the key-material fix, and with a pre-parsed key
under the stock library (medians of per-process medians). Each group is one
machine (Table~\ref{tab:machines}); absolute values are not comparable across
groups. The key-material fix was measured only on VM~B; its arm64 run is in
the replication package's list of pending experiments.}
\label{fig:remedies}
\end{figure}

\paragraph{The constraint} The \emph{success} of the parse on asymmetric key
material produces the key object whose type the key-confusion check depends
on. Removing the attempt for every string (the obvious optimisation) makes a
PEM public key configured where a secret is expected resolve as a secret, and
produces \SuiteNaiveFailing{} failures in the library's key-confusion tests
(\NaiveFailingTests). A fix must therefore skip the attempt only for key
material that cannot be asymmetric. The existing suite already guards the
property; what is missing is visibility of the coupling to someone changing
the code.

\paragraph{The narrow fix} Our first fix dispatches on the token's declared
algorithm: when the token declares an HMAC algorithm \emph{and} the secret is a
string with neither a PEM header nor a JSON object, the secret is resolved
directly. It takes the call from \HostJwtString~$\mu$s to
\HostJwtStringSafe~$\mu$s on the arm64 host, a factor of \HostSafePatchRatio,
with no change in calling code, and leaves the library's suite unchanged
(\SuitePatchedPassing{} passing, \SuitePatchedFailing{} failing).

\paragraph{The key-material fix} The declared algorithm is not needed. In
Node.js a string passed to \texttt{createPublicKey()} is parsed as PEM, so a
string with no PEM header can never produce a public key: for such a string the
stock library always reaches \texttt{createSecretKey()} through the exception.
Dispatching on the key material alone (a string with neither a PEM header nor a
JSON object goes straight to \texttt{createSecretKey()}, whatever the token
declares) therefore yields the same key object for every token, and keeps
everything that might be asymmetric material on the original path. We tested
this rather than relying on the argument. On each of \SuiteVariantRuntimes{}
runtimes the library's suite at \LibraryTag{} gives \SuiteVarKeyonlyPassing{}
passing and \SuiteVarKeyonlyFailing{} failing under this fix, as under the stock
library and the narrow fix, and \SuiteVarKeyonlyPlusPassing{} passing with our
four additional key-path tests; the unrestricted optimisation gives
\SuiteVarNaiveFailing{} failures on every runtime. On the same machine (VM~B,
Node \VmbNode, OpenSSL \VmbOpenssl) the key-material fix takes the call from
\VmbJwtString~$\mu$s to \VmbJwtStringKeyonly~$\mu$s, against
\VmbJwtStringSafe~$\mu$s for the narrow fix and \VmbJwtPreparsed~$\mu$s with a
pre-parsed key (Figure~\ref{fig:remedies}). What preserves the defence is the
restriction on key material, not the declared algorithm; the naive
optimisation fails because it drops that restriction.

\subsection{What the fixes leave reachable}\label{sec:reachable}

\begin{table}[!t]
\caption{Which tokens reach the discarded parse, for a service configured with
an HMAC shared secret, as read from the source at \LibraryTag{} and the patches
of Section~\ref{sec:fix}, and confirmed by the measurements of
Table~\ref{tab:forged}. ``Well-formed'': three segments, JSON header and
payload, non-empty signature. No row requires knowledge of the secret.}
\label{tab:reach}
\small
\begin{tabular}{@{}p{0.34\linewidth}p{0.6\linewidth}@{}}
\toprule
Configuration & Tokens that reach the parse \\
\midrule
Stock, string secret & every well-formed token, forged or genuine \\
Narrow fix, plain string secret (no PEM or JWK form) & every well-formed token whose header declares a
non-HMAC algorithm; no such token can be valid for this service \\
Key-material fix, plain string secret & none \\
Pre-parsed \texttt{KeyObject} & none \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

The narrow fix selects its fast path by the declared algorithm, which the
token's author chooses: a token declaring a non-HMAC algorithm falls through to
the original resolution and pays the parse before being rejected
(Table~\ref{tab:reach}). It removes the cost from legitimate traffic, not from
traffic an adversary constructs. The key-material fix and a pre-parsed key
object remove it for every input.

\paragraph{Measured} Table~\ref{tab:forged} times the rejection of well-formed
forged tokens, which a client can produce without the secret, under each
configuration (\texttt{bench/forged-token.js}; \ForgedInvocations{} processes
of \ForgedCalls{} calls per cell, on VM~B). The measurements confirm the source
reading. A token declaring RS256 is rejected by the algorithm list, yet under
the stock library and the narrow fix it first pays the discarded parse: on
Ubuntu 24.04's OpenSSL \ForgedUbuntuOpenssl{} \ForgedUbuntuRsString~$\mu$s and
\ForgedUbuntuRsSafe~$\mu$s, against \ForgedUbuntuRsKeyonly~$\mu$s under the
key-material fix and \ForgedUbuntuRsPreparsed~$\mu$s with a pre-parsed key. A
forged token declaring HS256 is cheap to reject under either fix. On
\texttt{node:26.6.0-alpine} an RS256-header rejection costs more than an HS256
one even with a pre-parsed key. The difference is V8's capture of the error's
stack trace at that throw site: run with stack capture disabled
(\texttt{--stack-trace-limit=0}), it falls from \RejTwentySixRsStack~$\mu$s to
\RejTwentySixRsNoStack~$\mu$s, while the HS256 rejection falls from
\RejTwentySixHsStack~$\mu$s to \RejTwentySixHsNoStack~$\mu$s; on the other three
runtimes the RS256 rejection is the cheaper of the two with or without stack
capture (\RejInvocations{} processes per cell). These are per-call costs in a
microbenchmark; we did not drive such tokens at a running service, and draw no
conclusion about availability.

\paragraph{Behaviour under misconfiguration} Both fixes take their fast path
only for a string that carries neither a PEM header nor a JSON object, so a PEM
or JWK key mistakenly configured as the HMAC ``secret'' resolves exactly as it
does today. We checked this rather than assuming it: for \EquivKeyKinds{} kinds
of configured key material (including PEM public and private keys, a PEM with
leading whitespace, a PEM inside a Buffer, and a JWK string supplied as the
secret), \EquivCasesPerRuntime{} combinations of key, token and algorithm option
were verified through the stock library and each fix on each of
\EquivRuntimes{} runtimes. \EquivDiffs{} produced a different result or error
under the narrow fix and \EquivDiffsKeyonly{} under the key-material fix
(\texttt{bench/keypath-equivalence.js}).

\subsection{Reported upstream}\label{sec:upstream}

An earlier issue\footnote{\url{https://github.com/auth0/node-jsonwebtoken/issues/966}}
reports HS256 verification in 9.x 34 times slower than in 8.5.1 on OpenSSL~3.0,
with no diagnosed cause. We reported the
mechanism\footnote{\url{https://github.com/auth0/node-jsonwebtoken/issues/1046}},
and a pull request implementing the narrow fix was opened against it; the
key-material fix of Section~\ref{sec:fix} is simpler and closes the gap the
narrow fix leaves, and we recommend it upstream.

Table~\ref{tab:reach}; Figs.~\ref{fig:verifyorder}, \ref{fig:remedies} &

\paragraph{Application developers} Pre-parse key material once, at startup
(Figure~\ref{fig:preparse}). It removes \HostStringPenalty~$\mu$s per
validation on the host and far more on OpenSSL~3.0, needs no architectural
change and no change to the library, and is the only remedy that removes the
discarded parse for every input. Also restrict permitted algorithms~\citep{rfc8725};
that is an independent defence, not a substitute.

\begin{figure}[!t]
\begin{lstlisting}[numbers=none]
const { createSecretKey } = require('node:crypto');
const jwt = require('jsonwebtoken');

// Once, at startup: build the key object.
const key = createSecretKey(Buffer.from(process.env.JWT_SECRET));

// Per request: pass the key object instead of the string.
jwt.verify(token, key, { algorithms: ['HS256'] });
\end{lstlisting}
\caption{The one-line change that removes the discarded parse for every input:
the secret is converted to a \texttt{KeyObject} once, and \texttt{verify()}
skips key resolution when handed one (Figure~\ref{fig:codepath}, line 120).}
\label{fig:preparse}
\end{figure}

\paragraph{Performance engineers} Treat the base image as part of the
measurement. The same code differs by \SpanProbeThrows$\times$ on this path
across images because they pin different OpenSSL releases, and a regression
after a base-image bump may have nothing to do with the application. Profile
before relocating a cost believed to be cryptographic to a sidecar or gateway.

\paragraph{Library authors} Do not use a failing parse as a type test. Inspect
and dispatch, refuse ambiguous input, or type the key, and resolve keys once
rather than on every call.

\paragraph{Maintainers and reviewers} Resolve a plain string secret directly,
keeping anything that might be asymmetric material on the original path: the
key-material fix of Section~\ref{sec:fix} is a change of a few lines. More
generally, review performance changes to verification code as security
changes, run them against the key-confusion tests, and time them on the oldest
cryptographic library a deployment may bundle.

%% ============================================================================
\section{Threats to validity}\label{sec:threats}

\paragraph{Construct} The decomposition relies on differencing, cross-checked
by a profiler whose share differs from the differenced one for the reasons
given in Section~\ref{sec:residual}. The C probe reproduces Node's OpenSSL
calls but not Node's own build of OpenSSL, so the binding column of
Table~\ref{tab:decomp} is approximate; the causal claim compares releases under
one build and does not inherit this. Every measurement uses HS256 with one
secret of 34 characters and one token of fixed size. The parse fails at the
PEM-header check and in the private-key decoder, and its cost does not depend
on the secret's length: a 16- and a 256-character secret cost
\ForgedEighteenProbeSixteen~$\mu$s and \ForgedEighteenProbeTwoFiftySix~$\mu$s on
OpenSSL \ForgedEighteenOpenssl{} (Section~\ref{sec:reachable}). A secret that
begins with a PEM header takes the original path under both fixes by design
and was not timed. The security analysis is from source, the library's tests
and the microbenchmarks of Section~\ref{sec:reachable}, not from adversarial
traffic against a service.

\paragraph{Internal} The in-situ evidence is one process sweeping seven rates
twice, and the A/B is one pair of consecutive windows at different host load
with the load generator on the same machine. CPU accounting excludes queueing
delay, but contention for caches, SMT siblings and processor frequency can still
raise the CPU time charged for the same work, so the A/B difference is an upper
bound on the work and carries no interval. An alternating design with the load
generator pinned or remote is prepared in the replication package but was not
run. The headline host figure predates the per-measurement OpenSSL field; its
version (\HostOpensslInferred) is inferred from the run record, and a re-run
with the version recorded is prepared.

\paragraph{External} Primary measurements come from one ARM64 host; the
x86\_64 machines are shared virtual machines, used only for orderings and
ratios. The containerised service is a single-node testbed on an end-of-life
Node~18 image; the OpenSSL~3.0 behaviour it shows is also present in Ubuntu
24.04's own Node.js (Section~\ref{sec:distro}), but the service itself was not
re-measured on a supported image. A service that caches verified tokens pays
the cost once per token. Seven libraries at one version each show a design
choice; the npm survey of Section~\ref{sec:libsurvey} estimates how often a
failing parse is used as a type test within a stated frame of one ecosystem,
not across ecosystems.

\paragraph{Reliability of the survey} Call-site buckets are assigned by rules
that trace a key within one file, and the counter-search and the library-survey
hits were adjudicated by one person. A blinded, stratified sheet of call sites,
a codebook and an agreement script for a second rater are in the replication
package; the second rating has not yet been done.

\paragraph{Future work} Driving forged tokens at the running service, repeating
the A/B as alternating windows on supported images, bisecting OpenSSL between
3.0 and 3.2, and extending the library survey to PyPI, Go and Maven would each
close a limitation stated above.

%% ============================================================================
\section{Conclusion}\label{sec:conclusion}

The per-request cost of token validation in \LibraryName{} is not the
signature (\HostHmacString~$\mu$s of \HostJwtString~$\mu$s) and not key
conversion (\HostCreateSecretKey~$\mu$s). It is a parse attempted in the wrong
order and discarded on every request, \HostProbeShareOfCall\% of the call. Its
price is set causally by the OpenSSL release beneath the runtime:
\CFullVThreeZeroSixteen~$\mu$s on \CVersionLiteralVThreeZeroSixteen{} against
\CFullVThreeFiveEight~$\mu$s on \CVersionLiteralVThreeFiveEight, and the slow
case persists in the Node.js that Ubuntu 24.04 ships. Per-call key handling is
a design choice, not a property of JWT; \LibraryName{} is distinguished by
making it through a failing parse, whose cost changes by an order of magnitude
with the OpenSSL release. That
parse cannot be removed naively, because it is load-bearing for a key-confusion
defence, and it is the restriction on key material, not the token's declared
algorithm, that the defence needs: a fix that dispatches on the key material
alone passes the library's suite, behaves identically to the stock library in
every case we tested, and removes the parse for every token. Until such a fix
ships, pre-parsing the key once achieves the same, yet no call site in our
sample does so.

The broader lesson is about attribution. The explanation that presented itself
before measurement was wrong twice, and the component that sets the cost is
one that measurement protocols rarely record. Performance studies should record
the identity of the components they measure, including transitive dependencies
such as the bundled cryptographic library, at the granularity at which they can
change.
